title: Japanese toilet aims to attract foreign tourists but not everybody is happy about it
description: Rural town’s attempt to draw tourists may have gone a step too far. In recent years, Japanese public toilets have become known not only as places to do your business but as tourist attractions with creative design features. So you can’t really blame the Kagawa Prefectural Government when they saw an opportunity to turn a […]
content:
Rural town’s attempt to draw tourists may have gone a step too far.

In recent years, Japanese public toilets have become known not only as places to do your business but as tourist attractions with creative design features. So you can’t really blame the Kagawa Prefectural Government when they saw an opportunity to turn a local public toilet into a tourist magnet. However, the resulting facility turned out to be so extravagant that it became a source of division instead.

The new building was unveiled to the public on 22 March outside JR Kinashi Station in Takamatsu, Kagawa Prefecture. During the official opening ceremony at the site that night, the mood was high, with government officials hailing it as a much-needed improvement to the previous outdated building, which housed a unisex, squat-style pit toilet that had long elicited complaints from residents over its poor condition and hygiene.

▼ This report shows the opening ceremony and the state of the former facilities.

When the station’s operators, JR Shikoku, said it would prefer to remove the facility altogether rather than rebuild it due to a lack of funds, prefectural officials stepped in with a plan to build a new public toilet, in order to serve the station’s approximately 600 daily boarding passengers, as well as students from a nearby prefectural high school who often stop to use the facilities.

▼ Kinashi Station sits two stops west of Takamatsu Station on the JR Yosan Line and ranks 14th out of Kagawa Prefecture’s 48 JR stations by passenger numbers.

The new building now contains separate men’s, women’s, and multi-purpose toilets with modern amenities, which locals have expressed appreciation for. The real wow factor, though, is the exterior, which acts as a canvas for two nightly projection mapping shows, held from 7:15 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. and again from 8:20 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. Weekday displays feature illuminated angel wings, while weekends showcase a rotating selection of different artworks, including student-produced videos.

While the light display has turned the public toilet into an eye-catching landmark, it also aims to help nurture young creators, with local students and emerging artists encouraged to submit their own projection mapping designs, giving them a rare opportunity to see their work displayed publicly.

Officials also hope the unusual attraction will encourage more visitors to stop by the area. As Japan’s leading producer of pine bonsai, Kinashi already attracts international visitors interested in the local craft, so it’s hoped that word of the unique building will spread amongst overseas travellers, helping to bring more tourism to the area.

Despite these admirable goals, the unusual concept has been attracting the wrong kind of attention, as many locals have been surprised to learn that the entire project reportedly cost around 100 million yen (US$670,000).

Local opinion over the cost has been divided, with some residents arguing that the money could have been better spent elsewhere, while others say the discussion itself has helped to shine a spotlight on the town and its attractions.

Like any revitalisation project, the return on investment may take some time to reveal itself, so we’ll have to wait and see whether this expensive toilet has the power to breathe new life into the town. One thing is certain, though – it’s certainly helped put Kinashi Station on the map by making headlines, and if you’d like to help support the town, you now know where to stop and do your business.

Sources: Kagawa Prefectural Government, Asahi Shimbun via Yahoo! Japan News (1, 2, 3)

title: End of a manga era as Weekly Shonen Jump’s circulation drops under one million
description: Weekly Shonen Jump is still the biggest magazine in Japan, but its print circulation is getting smaller and smaller. For decades, the jewel in the crown of the manga magazine world has been Weekly Shonen Jump. However, these days the jewel isn’t shining nearly as brightly as it used to, with the latest statistics showing […]
content:
Weekly Shonen Jump is still the biggest magazine in Japan, but its print circulation is getting smaller and smaller.

For decades, the jewel in the crown of the manga magazine world has been Weekly Shonen Jump. However, these days the jewel isn’t shining nearly as brightly as it used to, with the latest statistics showing that publisher Shueisha’s anthology has crossed over a significant threshold.

The Japan Magazine Publishers Association has released circulation data for the first quarter of the Japanese business year (April to June). During that time, Weekly Shonen Jump’s average print circulation fell to 985,000 copies per week. Not only was that a 1.9-percent drop compared to the preceding three-month period, it’s the first time since 2008 for Weekly Shonen Jump’s circulation to slip below one million, and possibly even longer since that’s as far back as regularly publicized circulation for the magazine goes.

The magazine’s weekly circulation peaked in late 1994 at a towering 6.53 million copies, which is an all-time high not only for Weekly Shonen Jump itself but for any manga anthology in the industry. At the time, it was the home of both Dragon Ball and Slam Dunk, iconic hit series with extremely broad fan bases whose creators were pumping out new chapters every week. By 2017 circulation dipped under two million, though, and just under a decade later, it’s roughly half of that.

Weekly Shonen Jump’s is still, however, the biggest manga magazine in Japan, and by a large margin. Its closest rival is publisher Kodansha’s Weekly Shonen Magazine, which has an average circulation of 281,000 copies for the most recent period. Next comes Shueisha’s own Weekly Young Jump (aimed at older readers in the seinen demographic) at 214,000 and just behind it is Shogakukan’s Monthly CoroCoro Comic, with 213,333. Circulation for Shogakukan’s biggest weekly manga anthology, Weekly Shonen Sunday, is 120,000. Meanwhile, in the shojo manga demographic aimed at young girls, no magazine has a six-figure circulation, with Shueisha’s monthly Ribon’s 90,000 copies being the highest. Average circulation dropped for almost all of these publications in the most recent period, with the exceptions of Weekly Shonen Sunday, whose numbers were unchanged, and Monthly CoroCoro Comic, with an increase of 1.6 percent.

▼ Ribon

Weekly Shonen Jump also remains the highest-circulation print magazine, of any type, in Japan, but that status also means that Japan no longer has any magazines with a circulation of a million copies.

Weekly Shonen Jump’s dwindling circulation doesn’t mean that Shueisha, or the manga creators whose series the company serializes, are on the ropes, however. A big part of why demand for the print version of the anthology is dropping is because Japanese manga publishers and consumers alike have enthusiastically embraced digital distribution platforms. Circulation falling below one million isn’t so much a sign that people have lost interest in manga as it is that people are very interested in reading manga on their phones or other devices, and the convenience of being able to read manga digitally is undeniably a benefit to people living in neighborhoods where they don’t have easy access to a brick-and-mortar retailer or people who are too busy to make manga shopping runs on a weekly basis.

On the other hand, a strong digital shift has a negative effect on retailers who sell print manga, and while convenience stores and train station kiosks can rely on revenue from other products, the paper manga fading away is going to hit bookstores hard.

Some have also voiced concerns about whether digital publishing can make it harder for readers to discover new series. With a printed magazine, there’s a mindset that since you’ve paid for the issue, you may as well take a look at every series inside, even ones you haven’t heard of or read before, and doing so is as quick and easy as flipping a page. The vaster variety of titles within a digital manga app presents a greater threat of choice paralysis, where a reader is overwhelmed with options and so falls back on a familiar favorite rather than giving something new a shot, so manga’s increasingly digital future might require a bit more conscious effort on readers’ part to dive into a chapter of something they’ve never read before.

Source: Japan Magazine Publishers Association (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7), TBS News Dig via Livedoor News, Yomiuri Shimbun

title: Studio Ghibli unveils new finger puppets featuring anime characters from My Neighbour Totoro
description: Recreate magical movie moments with beloved characters on your fingertips. When you become an adult you don’t always have to give up your childlike sense of fun and adventure, and Studio Ghibli is here to remind us of that fact with a new range of beautifully designed finger puppets. Called My Neighbour Totoro Soft Vinyl […]
content:
Recreate magical movie moments with beloved characters on your fingertips.

When you become an adult you don’t always have to give up your childlike sense of fun and adventure, and Studio Ghibli is here to remind us of that fact with a new range of beautifully designed finger puppets.

Called My Neighbour Totoro Soft Vinyl Mascot Finger Puppets, this collection consists of 11 different puppets, starring eight characters from My Neighbour Totoro.

Released by Ghibli specialty retailer Donguri Kyowakoku, the collection is the newest addition to the chain’s popular Sofubi Mascot Finger Puppet series, with “Sofubi” (ソフビ) used to mean “soft vinyl”.

Each puppet measures approximately 3.8 × 4.9 × 2.2 centimetres (1.5 × 1.9 × 0.9 inches) and weighs just 12 grams (0.4 ounces), making them light and easy to use for both adults and children.

Taking a closer look at the range, we have two sets dedicated to the titular character and the smaller of its species.

▼ They’re as cute from behind as they are from the front.

▼ Large Totoro

▼ Medium Totoro

▼ Small Totoro

The second set of Totoros recalls the magical night scene where they can be seen blowing into their musical ocarinas.

▼ Large Totoro Ocarina

▼ Medium Totoro Ocarina

▼ Small Totoro Ocarina

No collection from My Neighbour Totoro would truly be complete without an appearance from two members of the supporting cast, who are beautifully captured in miniature form.

▼ The Catbus…

▼ …and the Soot Sprites.

Rounding out the collection are three members from the human cast.

▼ Satsuki…

▼ … Kanta…

▼ … and Mei.

While all the characters above are ready to play out imaginative scenarios from the tips of your fingers, they’re so well sculpted that they make equally beautiful decorations.

Sure, the size discrepancies might mean that Mei has a harder time swatting the Soot Sprites between the palms of her hands…

▼… and the way she towers over the Catbus has it looking more like the Kittenbus…

▼ … but all these quirks can be reconciled with a little twist of the imagination.

A range this cute is likely to sell out fast, especially as each character puppet is reasonably priced at 770 yen (US$4.86). So be sure to hunt them down at your nearest branch of Donguri Kyowakoku in Japan, or keep your finger poised and ready to hit the purchase button when sales commence online at 10 a.m. on 8 August.

Source: Donguri Kyowakoku

title: Anime fan in Japan arrested for ordering and cancelling over 4.3 billion yen in anime merch
description: Shop ‘till you drop unfortunately becomes shop ‘till you get arrested. As any hard-core fan can tell you, anime and manga can be a pricey hobby. Sure, the proliferation of video streaming services and digital reader apps mean the content itself is much more affordable than it used to be, but the modern otaku merchandising […]
content:
Shop ‘till you drop unfortunately becomes shop ‘till you get arrested.

As any hard-core fan can tell you, anime and manga can be a pricey hobby. Sure, the proliferation of video streaming services and digital reader apps mean the content itself is much more affordable than it used to be, but the modern otaku merchandising industry is more robust than ever, with an endless flow of figures, plushies, character standees, and more for fans to covet.

This brings us to a 32-year-old restaurant worker living in Osaka’s Kita Ward, who, in a statement to the police, said “I like anime,” and has the numerical data to back it up. Over a roughly two-year period beginning around October of 2023, she ordered more than 4.3 billion yen (US$27 million) worth of items from manga publisher Shueisha’s Jump Character Store. If you’re wondering how she managed to pay for all that merch on what’s assumedly a modest food service worker’s salary, the answer is that she didn’t.

That’s not to say that the woman, Mayu Yoshida, stole anything. Instead, she placed the orders but never paid for, or took delivery of, the items. She did this through two methods, the first of which involved exploiting Japan’s convenience store prepayment system. For shoppers who either don’t have a credit card or don’t want to carry a balance on it, many online retailers in Japan allow customers to place an order but pay for it at a convenience store, with the seller shipping the item once payment has been confirmed. There’s a limit, though, to how much time is allowed to pass between the order’s placement and payment, after which the order will be cancelled. So Yoshida would order figures, key chains, and other items through the Jump Character Shop, select the convenience store prepayment method, and just never actually go to pay for them. Between 2024 and 2025, she placed orders with a total bill of over 4.3 billion yen this way.

Her second strategy was to order items from the Jump Character Shop and select the cash-on-delivery payment method, wherein the recipient renders payment to the delivery person. In these instances, Yoshida would refuse delivery, and therefore not pay for, the things she’d ordered. It’s unclear what the total value was for the orders she refused delivery of, but you have to wonder if any delivery person got tired of coming to her house again and again.

▼ Please, ma’am, I’m begging you, pay for this one.

As a major online retailer, the Jump Character Store likely has protocols in place to flag orders from shoppers who habitually cancel or refuse delivery of their orders, but Yoshida got around these safeguards by creating 238 different customer accounts and hopping from one to another.

However, just because she wasn’t keeping any of the items without paying for them doesn’t make this a no-harm, no-foul situation. By not paying for the COD items, she also wasn’t paying for the shipping charges, leaving Shueisha with a cumulative bill of approximately 7.5 million yen in fees for items sent to her which then had to be returned. There’re also restocking and order-processing costs involved, all of which were enough for the police to arrest Yoshida on charges of fraudulent obstruction of business, which she has admitted to, on August 4.

The repeated targeting of the Jump Character Store might make it seem like she has a bone to pick with the manga magazine or its publisher, but that’s actually not the case. “I have been feeling stressed from daily life, and I felt a sense of satisfaction and refreshment from ordering items before they sold out,” said Yoshida following her arrest. “I do not have any resentment towards Shueisha.”

A particularly bittersweet aspect to the situation is that Yoshida had previously been a legitimate paying customer with the Jump Character Store, placing her first order in the fall of 2018. Hopefully once her legal situation is sorted out she’ll be able to return to a more responsible form of fandom.

Sources: FNN Prime Online, Jiji, Yomiuri Shimbun

title: 7-Eleven Japan rethinks convenience store drinks with new Grilled Corn Chilled Soup Smoothie
description: Exclusive to only two wards in Tokyo, this is a must-try drink that’s very hard to get. We’re always on the lookout for new and unusual convenience store finds in Japan, so when 7-Eleven announced it would be releasing a never-before-seen chilled soup smoothie made with grilled corn, we knew it was something we had […]
content:
Exclusive to only two wards in Tokyo, this is a must-try drink that’s very hard to get.

We’re always on the lookout for new and unusual convenience store finds in Japan, so when 7-Eleven announced it would be releasing a never-before-seen chilled soup smoothie made with grilled corn, we knew it was something we had to try.

Finding it, however, proved to be more challenging than we’d thought, as it’s currently only available at select 7-Eleven stores in Tokyo’s Chuo and Chiyoda wards. After visiting four stores in Chuo without any luck, we eventually found it at our fifth stop, where a huddle of them were lying in wait like golden treasures, gleaming at us from inside the standing freezer section.

▼ A huddle sounds like a good collective noun for smoothies.

After plucking one out and paying for it at the register, we headed over to the smoothie machine at the counter, where we scanned the barcode on the lid before tearing it off to look inside.

▼ 冷製スープ = Chilled Soup

▼ There, in the cup, we found… actual pieces of grilled corn!

The corn looked good enough to eat right away but we were here to drink it, so we popped the cup into the machine and waited for it to work its magic. With apple and banana puree also in the mix, we were curious to find out what this soup-smoothie fusion would taste like, and when it was ready, we were fascinated by the way the corn had totally disappeared and become liquid, with tiny dark grilled flecks being the only evidence of its existence.

Taking a sip, it was clear that the corn was the star of the show. Coupled with fermented rice bran, made with lactic acid bacteria and yeast for gut health, and oligosaccharides to bring out the richness and sweetness of the vegetable, the corn flavour was sweet, with a subtle smokiness, making it different to the cans of corn potage that usually come to mind when we think of a Japanese-style corn soup.

While corn potage balances sweet and savoury flavours, this variety veers towards sweetness, which is apt seeing as it’s marketed as a smoothie. In fact, as we sipped our way through the drink, we found our taste buds becoming confused over whether this should be classed as a soup or a smoothie, as the grilled vegetable component made us think we were having soup, but the overriding sweetness made us think we were drinking a smoothie.

▼ Despite the addition of fruit puree, the smoothie doesn’t taste fruity at all, making it very different from all the other fresh smoothies at 7-Eleven.

At nearly 500 yen (US$3.19), it’s also one of the most expensive smoothies in the range, and one of the hardest to find, given its very limited availability. Though there’s no word yet on whether the smoothies will expand beyond the two Tokyo wards where it’s currently being sold, this is one of the chain’s most unusual and exciting creations, and well worth trying if you’re able to find it.

As part of 7-Eleven’s latest push to explore unexpected flavour combinations and challenge our expectations of convenience store food, this is a taste odyssey we’re happy to be on, and we can’t wait to see what weird and wonderful places the chain takes us with its next new release.

title: Beautiful Totoro bonsai figure needs no watering, makes soothing rain showers whenever you want
description: Need a stress-soothing break? This figurine’s return means you can wait with Totoro while he waits for the Cat Bus. A bonsai tree can be a great way to add some picturesque tranquility to your home or work/study space. However, bonsai often require complex care routines, and if you don’t have much of a green […]
content:
Need a stress-soothing break? This figurine’s return means you can wait with Totoro while he waits for the Cat Bus.

A bonsai tree can be a great way to add some picturesque tranquility to your home or work/study space. However, bonsai often require complex care routines, and if you don’t have much of a green thumb, the hassle and stress of keeping one healthy can undo the sense of calm relaxation you were longing for.

So today let’s take a look at an alternative kind of bonsai that, in addition to being easier to care for, also has the major advantage of coming with Totoro.

Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku has restocked its previously sold-out My Neighbor Totoro Water Garden Bonsai, which carries the subtitle of “Kasayadori.” Kasayadori refers to taking shelter from the rain, especially under the boughs of a tree, and that’s exactly what Totoro is doing in this recreation of the scene from the anime movie where he’s waiting for the Catbus to come by.

The Totoro factor isn’t the only thing that separates this from a conventional bonsai tree, either, because this figurine can make its own weather.

Drawing power from an attached USB cord, the Water Garden Bonsai functions as a desktop fountain, with rivulets pouring down around Totoro and Mei.

The clever design means that once the water falls, it gets picked up in the base of the figurine…

…and cycled back up into the upper part to fall again, so there’s no need to refill it every time you want the soothing sound of rain.

Though big sister Satsuki is absent from the scene, Mei and Totoro are joined by a friendly frog, Soot Sprites in the tree branches, and a small Totoro with a leaf for an umbrella, who wobbles as the rain falls on him.

The fountain effect can be turned on and left to run indefinitely, or set to a “voice-activated” mode that will cause rain to fall for a five-minute cycle.

▼ A video showing the fountain turned in action

Unfortunately, the other Ghibli bonsai-style water gardens shown in the video are no longer available, but the Totoro Kasayadori version, which is 22 centimeters (8.7 inches) tall and priced at 17,600 yen (US$112) is once again available for order through the Donguri Kyowakoku online store here.
